title: A Handwriting Routine: As Little Support as Possible, As Much as Needed
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: The author profiles first-grade teacher Stephane Bolton's handwriting routine, built on the EBLI Handwriting for Fluency Protocol with Peterson Handwriting prompts, in which students retrieve letter shapes from memory rather than copying or tracing them. Support is deliberately minimal and fades quickly, moving from verbal prompts to modeling to dot/arrow cues to hand-over-hand assistance only as a last resort. The piece frames Bolton's guiding phrase, 'as little support as possible but as much as needed for success,' as a broader instructional philosophy the author wants to carry into the new school year across reading and writing tasks alike. The underlying argument is that genuine skill-building requires students to do the retrieval work themselves, with teachers providing scaffolded feedback rather than doing the cognitive lifting for them.
points: The routine's key design choice is retrieval over copying: students write the lowercase alphabet from memory rather than tracing, after having already received direct instruction in proper letter formation.
Support is sequenced from lightest to heaviest and fades as quickly as possible: verbal prompts, then modeling, then dot/arrow cues, with hand-over-hand support reserved as a genuine last resort.

Bolton's guiding phrase, 'as little support as possible but as much as needed for success,' is offered as a transferable philosophy for reading and writing instruction generally, not just handwriting.

The author is explicit that this student-driven retrieval practice only works after clear, direct instruction and ample teacher modeling have already happened, rejecting a false choice between explicit instruction and independent practice.
quotes: I would argue that a big part of being a teacher is figuring how to appropriately balance necessary instruction with useful practice (neither too easy nor too hard).

This routine is different from many other handwriting routines because students do NOT copy and trace letters. Rather, they retrieve the letter shapes from memory and then write them, using correct formation.
I like this routine because the student is doing the real work and practicing the thing she needs to do: writing letters efficiently, accurately, automatically, and independently.
In Stephane's words, this routine is all about giving "as little support as possible but as much needed for success.
Whenever possible, we want students doing the heavy lifting, whether that's writing letters from memory, reading a decodable text, reading an uncontrolled text, or writing a paragraph.
Of course, before they do this heavy lifting, students need clear, direct instruction and ample modeling from their teachers.
